title: Solar Neutrino Problem
body:
Fusion in the Sun's core produces neutrinos as well as light, and neutrinos escape immediately
where light takes tens of thousands of years to diffuse out. Counting them is therefore a
direct measurement of what the core is doing right now, which makes it the sharpest test of the
[[Main Sequence]] model available.

The Homestake experiment began counting in the late 1960s and measured about one third of the
predicted flux. The disagreement held for three decades and was too large to be error.

Three possible explanations, and the course uses this as its example of how a discrepancy gets
resolved:

```
the model of the Sun is wrong        the core is cooler than believed
the detector is wrong                systematic error in a hard measurement
the neutrinos are wrong              something happens to them in transit
```

The third turned out to be correct. Neutrinos come in three types, the detectors could see only
one, and neutrinos oscillate between types on the way from the Sun. About two thirds arrived as
types the experiment could not register.

The resolution changed particle physics and left the solar model intact, because oscillation
requires neutrinos to have mass, which the standard model had assumed they lacked. The solar
model survived unchanged, which is the outcome that makes the episode worth teaching: an
anomaly in one field was a discovery in another.
